THE ULTIMATE GUIDE TO CRAFTING EFFECTIVE WEBSITE REDESIGN RFPS

 * October 26, 2026

 * IA, Design, Strategy, Development, Analytics, Web Development


You need a new website now, but you have a nagging feeling that the internet is going to look and feel like a very different place in a few years. Search is changing rapidly. Prospective students are asking ChatGPT or reading Google's AI Overviews about you before they visit. But you still need a new site. And you need to write an RFP to find the right partner to help build it.


Last year we covered some RFP basics: outcomes over deliverables, real budgets, published weighting. This time we wanted to go section by section through what an RFP needs to contain, what to ask potential partners, especially with so many technology changes happening so rapidly. There is a downloadable website redesign RFP template at end to help get you started.


UNDERSTANDING RFPS


WHAT IS A WEBSITE REDESIGN RFP?

A website redesign RFP (request for proposal) is the document a college, university or nonprofit issues to invite agencies to propose on a website project. You will also see it called a web design RFP or a website development RFP; same thing. At its simplest, it gives potential partners your current situation, your goals, your approximate budget, your timeline, and your selection criteria. They respond with a proposal: their approach, their team, their price.

It is your one chance to articulate to a bunch of vendors what you are trying to do clearly enough that they can provide a scope, timeline, process and cost. 

> You are hiring a partner precisely because you don’t know the solution yet.


WHY THE RFP MATTERS IN WEB DEVELOPMENT

The RFP sets the stage for everything that follows. A vague RFP tends to get vague proposals, and a vague proposal becomes a contract with a lot of assumptions baked into it. And nobody wants that…

Budgets make this hard. Budgeting cycles mean RFPs often have to ask for a fixed bid, even when the project isn’t very defined. And that is fair, because you are hiring a partner precisely because you don’t know the solution yet. We’ve read recent RFPs that ask the agency to recommend a CMS and, in the same document, give a fixed price for the build. Nobody can price a build on a platform that hasn’t been chosen. You can try…but you are going to receive numbers that are padded or full of assumptions. Most of what follows is about avoiding that.

> You can’t price a site build on an undefined platform .


KEY COMPONENTS OF A WEBSITE REDESIGN RFP


EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

A good opening is one page a potential partner can read quickly and understand the ask: who you are, what the project entails, why now, roughly what you can spend, and when proposals are due. Include the drivers behind the project: enrollment is down in two programs, the site is on a platform that is going end of life, the brand just changed. Partners write better proposals when they know your goals.

Also, state the unknowns. It is okay to not know everything. You may not be able to get a super accurate fixed bid if, say, you don’t actually know what CMS you want to be on, but it is better to be transparent and hear from a swath of potential partners about how they would help you make those decisions than to let partners ‘throw spaghetti at the wall and see what sticks’.

> A 450-page site on twelve feature-rich templates and a 450-page newsroom site require different levels of effort.


PROJECT SCOPE AND GOALS

Start with goals. Framing them as the outcomes you need instead of the features you want gives agencies a chance to show you how they would meet those goals, and you may find some surprising, creative opportunities in the answers. “Increase inquiries from prospective graduate students” is a goal. “A program finder” is one of several ways to get there.

Then say what success looks like. Goals tell an agency where you want to go; a short list of indicators tells them how you will know you got there, and it turns “is the new site working?” from a feeling into a question with an answer. Three to six is plenty: inquiries and applications started from the site, whether a prospective student can find a program’s deadline and cost in a couple of clicks, whether AI search tools cite your pages for program questions, accessibility conformance after launch, how long it takes an editor to publish a page. Capture a baseline before launch so there is something to compare against. Agencies will propose better measurement approaches if they know what you plan to measure, and it sets up the reporting conversation later in the RFP.

Then scope. This is often where an RFP loses the plot: it gives a page count with no sense of the features, functionality or complexity behind it. It helps a lot to describe the site in page templates and features, not just pages. A 450-page site on twelve templates and a 450-page site that is mostly basic content with no unique features are different jobs, and “approximately 450 pages” on its own tells an agency very little. Think carefully about the content, too. Migrating it, rewriting it and writing it new are three different levels of effort, and if the RFP doesn’t say how you want content handled, agencies will make a lot of assumptions.

If the platform is undecided, we think the better move is to split the work. A short discovery RFP for research, maybe a content model, a platform recommendation and a scoped plan can help. The design and development RFP can then be fixed price. It feels like an extra step, but in our experience it gets you a clearer budget.

> A site organized around the org chart serves nobody.


BUDGET CONSIDERATIONS

Be transparent with your budget. It helps everyone. It keeps vendors who cannot work within your budget from responding. With a number in hand, partners can tell you what it is possible and where you may have to make trade-offs. If you can’t publish a figure, publish a range, and say whether it includes CMS licensing, hosting and third-party fees. Our redesign cost post has ranges if you need a starting point.

It also helps to outline what can be budgeted separately: the post-launch retainer, any AI chatbot, content writing beyond a set number of pages, photography. If you ask for those as priced options so you can decide on those a la carte. 

> Without a budget, vendors guess, and the guesses range so widely that the proposals cannot be compared.


TIMELINE AND MILESTONES

It helps to give two timelines. The procurement timeline and the project timeline. The procurement timeline includes: issue date, question deadline, when answers are published, proposal deadline, interviews, notice of selection. In our experience it is a few months from first draft to signed contract, longer at public institutions, so it is worth working backward from there.

The project timeline is tricky because you are asking your future partner to agree to a timeline before they really know your working style and your team’s availability. Share the constraints that are real: the admissions cycle, commencement, an accreditation visit, a platform contract that expires. Give a desired launch and say whether it is a hope or a hard date. Then ask each agency for their milestones and, more usefully, the decisions and materials they will need from you. 


CRAFTING YOUR WEBSITE DESIGN PROPOSAL


DEFINING YOUR TARGET AUDIENCE

Start by listing your audiences and their key goals on the site. Prospective undergraduates, their parents, transfer students, graduate prospects, current students, faculty and staff, alumni and donors, the community. 

It also helps to say which audiences are the priority, because they can’t all be. If you have research, attach it. If you don’t, that is okay too; just say so.


DESIGN CONCEPT EXPECTATIONS

We’d encourage you not to ask for design concepts in the proposal. Concepts produced in two weeks without research or your content are guesses, and they tend to reward the firm with the most free time rather than the best process. Case studies, an approach walkthrough and references will tell you more. If you really want to see design thinking before you sign, it is reasonable to pay a finalist for a short, scoped exercise.

> ‘The site must support AI’ is not a clear requirement.”


TECHNICAL SPECIFICATIONS AND REQUIREMENTS

Most website RFPs cover the technical basics well: CMS, hosting, responsive design, integrations. Five areas have changed in the last few years and are worth some extra attention. 

AI search. Prospective students now ask ChatGPT, Google’s AI Mode, Perplexity and Copilot about you, so your site needs to be readable and quotable by those tools. Writing “the site must support AI” in the RFP won’t get you that, because agencies read it two different ways: some will propose an AI product, like a chatbot or AI personalization tools, and others will propose making your content visible to AI search. Be clear about what you want. If it is AI search, ask each agency what they would do to your most important pages, how they would measure whether AI tools cite you compared with peer institutions, and what they would report 90 days after launch. (Our AI visibility and SEO and GEO pages describe this work, and GEO vs. SEO explains the thinking behind it.) If you also want a chatbot, a personalization engine, or embedded AI/conversational search in the site, ask for it as a separately priced option so you can see its cost on its own.

Content portability. Nobody knows which web platforms will matter in 2030, which makes committing to a content management system a somewhat anxiety provoking decision. Ask each agency to describe, in a page, how your content would be exported: in what format, how much effort it would take, and who owns the design system and code afterward. Ask, too, whether the content model (the definition of a course, a program, a person, an event) is documented separately from the CMS, so it can move with you. Structured content like that is also what AI search tools read best.

Accessibility. The standard to require is WCAG 2.2 AA, which has been current since October 2023. The ADA Title II web deadlines were extended in April 2026, to April 2027 for larger public entities and April 2028 for smaller ones.  Who on the agency team does accessibility testing, how do they test, and do they test with real assistive technology or only automated tools. (Here is how we approach accessibility, including testing with people who use assistive technology.)

Security and data. Your IT and procurement colleagues will need answers to these eventually, so it saves time to ask in the RFP. Does the agency hold a current SOC 2 Type 2 report, and will they share it under NDA? Where will your data be stored during the build? Which AI tools does the agency use in its own work, what of your content goes into them, and how long is it kept? We went through SOC 2 ourselves and it was a bit of a bear, but it means we now have a third-party verified report we can hand to a review committee.

Integrations. List every system the new site has to connect to: the CRM (Slate, Salesforce), the student information system, the course catalog, the events calendar, the giving platform, the directory. Ask each agency to state its assumptions and any third-party costs for each one. Integrations are the most common source of surprise costs in a fixed-price build, so the more detail you give here, the more accurate the proposals will be.

> Integrations are where fixed bids go to die.


EVALUATION CRITERIA FOR VENDORS


SCORING FRAMEWORK

We recommend publishing your scoring criteria and their weights in the RFP. Agencies write to what you score, and a committee that has agreed on a rubric before the proposals arrive has an easier time choosing. REQUEST FOR PROPOSALS: WEBSITE REDESIGN & ECOSYSTEM DEVELOPMENT

----------------------------------------

CATEGORY: Partnerships

Isabella Senzamici • Oct 6, 2026


SHARE THIS STORY



Digital Strategy, UX/UI Design, CMS Development, Migration, and Ongoing Technical Support

THE OPPORTUNITY AT A GLANCE



Achievement First is seeking an experienced digital agency to architect and build a unified, scalable digital ecosystem. The solution will comprise a main network website, regional hubs, and 41 distinct school-specific websites under a central governance model. 

 

RFP Key Milestones Date / Timeline RFP Issuance Date October 5, 2026 Vendor Questions Due October 19, 2026 Proposal Submission Deadline November 9, 2026 Finalist Presentations & Demonstrations November 16-20 & November 30-December 4, 2026 Target Selection Notification By December 11, 2026 Project Kickoff January 2027


1. EXECUTIVE OVERVIEW & BACKGROUND

Achievement First (AF) is a non-profit charter school network serving more than 15,000 students across 41 schools in Connecticut, New York, and Rhode Island. As our network evolves, our digital presence must effectively communicate our mission, advance our organizational goals, empower local school communities, and streamline stakeholder engagement.

AF is issuing this Request for Proposals (RFP) to select a qualified website strategy, design, and development partner to architect, redesign, rebuild, and migrate our primary digital footprint (currently hosted on WordPress at achievementfirst.org). In tandem with this web initiative, AF is finalizing an organization-wide visual brand refresh; the new digital platform will serve as the premier public presentation of our updated brand identity.

This initiative extends beyond a routine template redesign or standalone marketing site. AF requires a unified, flexible web ecosystem structured across three interdependent tiers:

 * Network Website: Representing Achievement First as a unified overarching organization.
 * Regional Hubs: Providing localized information, news, and regulatory resources for state and municipal contexts.
 * School Websites (41 Connected Micro Sites): Comprehensive pages for each school location within a single governed system, designed to adapt easily as schools open, expand, or relocate.


2. CONTEXT & OPPORTUNITY

Over years of rapid network growth, AF’s current website architecture has become fragmented. Prospective and current families encounter friction when identifying local schools or navigating enrollment pathways. Prospective educators experience challenges when applying for jobs. Donors and board members should be able to find the information they need and see clear opportunities to give and advocate for AF. Crucial school-level facts are often incomplete, while duplicated network-wide content creates operational overhead and risks content obsolescence.

The redesigned platform must deliver an exceptional user experience while introducing a sustainable content management model. Non-technical network and school staff must be empowered to publish routine updates easily within defined central guardrails for brand integrity, accessibility compliance, security, and performance.


3. PROJECT OBJECTIVES

 * User Experience: Deliver an intuitive, mobile-first design allowing key users to complete priority tasks rapidly.
 * Brand Cohesion: Establish a recognizable AF network brand experience while honoring distinct regional and local school identities.
 * Robust Local Sites: Provide each of the 41 schools with a connected robust, functional site rather than a basic landing page.
 * Streamlined Publishing: Enable intuitive content management for non-technical users across network, regional, and school levels.
 * Governance & Workflows: Implement role-based permissions, editorial review workflows, content expiration rules, and structured approval paths.
 * Single-Source Content: Utilize structured data models so shared school and regional attributes are updated once and rendered consistently across the ecosystem.
 * Strategic Goals Support: Drive measurable conversions for student enrollment, staff recruitment, family involvement, philanthropy, and advocacy, including personalized donor engagement paths tailored to interest areas and giving levels.
 * Compliance & Standards: Exceed industry benchmarks for WCAG 2.2 AA accessibility, multilingual localization, privacy, security, page speed, SEO, and Answer Engine Optimization (AEO).
 * Scalability: Build a technical architecture that expands seamlessly as new schools, integrations, or custom tools are introduced.


4. PRIORITY AUDIENCES

Key audiences include prospective and enrolled families, prospective and current staff, alumni, philanthropic partners, board members, community advocates, public school authorizers, and news media. Discovery will focus on optimizing user journeys for top-priority interactions rather than treating all pages and audiences equally.

The end-user experience must be heavily optimized for mobile devices, low-bandwidth connections, assistive technology devices, and multilingual users (primarily English and Spanish speakers).


5. DETAILED SCOPE OF WORK

The selected vendor will lead eight primary workstreams. Vendors should outline their proposed methodology, recommended technical stack, key assumptions, trade-offs, and explicit exclusions for each stream.


5.1 DISCOVERY, STRATEGY, & USER EXPERIENCE

 * Facilitate stakeholder alignment on goals, KPIs, audience prioritization, governance, and risk mitigation.
 * Perform comprehensive technical, content, SEO, accessibility, and analytics audits of the existing web footprint.
 * Conduct user research with key demographics including multilingual families, staff, and mobile users.
 * Develop information architecture, user flows, navigation structures, and search strategies.
 * Produce and usability-test interactive prototypes and responsive wireframes prior to front-end engineering.


5.2 VISUAL DESIGN & BRAND SYSTEM

 * Translate AF’s refreshed visual brand guidelines into an engaging, modern, and accessible digital design system.
 * Create responsive page designs across mobile, tablet, and desktop breakpoints for all tier templates.
 * Build a component-based design library enabling modular page creation without breaking layout rules.
 * Partner with AF’s internal design team and hand off fully documented Figma or equivalent design assets.


5.3 MULTI-TIER ARCHITECTURE & ECOSYSTEM STRUCTURE

The architecture must seamlessly support three connected tiers while maintaining central governance and eliminating redundant data entry:

 

Ecosystem Tier Scope & Functional Capabilities Network Level Overall mission, educational model, organizational stories, network leadership and boards, careers/recruitment, giving/philanthropy, press releases, and network-wide compliance resources. Regional Hubs Region-specific directory of schools, state and city enrollment guidelines, regional leadership, news, community partnerships, public notices, localized events, and targeted emergency alerts. 41 School Pages Dedicated pages for each school featuring local navigation, school leadership, academic programming, enrollment steps, school-level volunteer sign-up and management workflows, calendars, family portals, local news, and school geography and contact information.

The platform must allow AF administrators to provision, reconfigure, or archive school sites effortlessly as the network evolves, without requiring software developer intervention.


5.4 CONTENT STRATEGY, MIGRATION, & GOVERNANCE

 * Audit legacy web content, documents, media assets, active forms, and URL redirect patterns.
 * Develop a content migration strategy identifying content for retention, rewriting, consolidation, or archiving.
 * Define content taxonomies, structured fields, editorial ownership models, and review intervals.
 * Execute migration and QA for all approved network content, regional hubs, and all 41 school websites.
 * Configure granular role-based permissions (central admin, regional editor, school publisher) with approval workflows.
 * Enable cascading content distribution (e.g., syndicate a network update to all schools or specific regions).
 * Implement an organized document library for required school policies, forms, and regulatory disclosures.


5.5 CORE FUNCTIONALITY & TECHNICAL INTEGRATIONS

 * Find a School & Volunteer Portal: Interactive map and list interface with geolocation, grade-level filtering, school tour videos embedded, direct enrollment routing, and localized volunteer sign-up capabilities across individual school sites.
 * Site Search: Indexed global and scoped search across pages, documents, news, and school profiles with facet filters.
 * Forms & System Integration: Embed web forms connected to key third-party platforms (SchoolMint, HubSpot, Greenhouse, etc.).
 * Alert Banners: Targeted notification banners for emergency closures or notices at network, regional, or school levels.
 * Enhanced Funder & Donor Experience: Sophisticated, tiered donor pathways going beyond a single landing page to present customized content, impact stories, high-impact video storytelling capabilities, digital Annual Report (AR) vision integration, and engagement opportunities based on donor interest areas and giving levels.
 * Technical SEO & Answer Engine Optimization (AEO): Structured schema markup, XML sitemaps, semantic tags, automated redirect handling, and AEO strategies to optimize content discovery across AI search engines and conversational assistants.
 * Analytics & Tracking: Google Tag Manager & GA4 setup supporting rollup and property-level event/conversion reporting, including custom GA4 reports and event tracking dashboards tailored to core functional areas such as student enrollment and talent recruitment.

Current and anticipated integrations include SchoolMint/HubSpot (Enrollment CRM), Greenhouse (Careers), Salesforce & Fundraise Up (Fundraising), ParentSquare, Infinite Campus, Google Maps API, and Google Analytics. Vendors should detail experience integrating these or similar systems.


5.6 ACCESSIBILITY, LOCALIZATION, & WEB PERFORMANCE

 * WCAG 2.2 AA Compliance: Full adherence to WCAG 2.2 Level AA standards verified via automated tools and manual screen-reader/keyboard testing.
 * Multilingual Architecture: Seamless multi-language framework supporting human translations, intuitive language selectors, and localized metadata.
 * Document Accessibility: Strategy for handling non-compliant legacy PDFs/documents, identifying core scope vs. optional remediation.
 * Core Web Vitals Performance: Target mobile metrics at the 75th percentile: LCP ≤ 2.5s, INP ≤ 200ms, CLS ≤ 0.1.
 * Lighthouse Benchmarks: Target scores of 90+ across Performance, Accessibility, Best Practices, and SEO for key page templates.


5.7 PLATFORM, ARCHITECTURE, & SECURITY

 * CMS Selection: Recommend a modern, secure CMS (e.g., Enterprise WordPress, WordPress Multisite, Drupal, or Headless solution) suitable for non-profit scale.
 * Editing Experience: Structured block-based authoring experience preventing accidental layout breaking or accessibility non-compliance.
 * Security Protocols: Role-based access controls, SSO/MFA/SCIM capability, SSL, automated backups (vendor must specify backup frequency, retention period, and storage location [on-platform vs. offsite/geo-redundant]; minimum requirements include daily automated backups across all 41 school sites plus network and regional tiers, 30-day retention minimum, Recovery Point Objective [RPO] of 24 hours or less, and Recovery Time Objective [RTO] of 8 hours or less for full platform restore; vendor must describe restore process and confirm testing), vulnerability scanning, and DDoS protection.
 * Environments & Deployment: Isolated Dev, Staging, and Production environments with Git-based CI/CD deployment workflows.

INTRODUCTION 
The City of Saugatuck is a small but highly active waterfront community whose digital audience
extends well beyond its year-round population of approximately 865 residents. Covering
approximately 1.47 square miles with 11.5 miles of roads, the City serves a diverse audience of
residents, property owners, businesses, seasonal residents, voters, applicants, and visitors.
Saugatuck maintains approximately 500 acres of parks, natural areas, and recreational spaces,
including nationally recognized Oval Beach, Mt. Baldhead Park, the 173-acre Saugatuck Harbor
Natural Area, the approximately 169-acre Saugatuck Wilds Nature Preserve, and numerous
community parks and public spaces such as Coghlin Park, Wicks Park, Jones Park, Cook Park,
Willow Park, Peterson Preserve, and Village Square Park. These facilities, along with the City's
active calendar of events and seasonal activities, make the City website an essential resource
for communicating municipal services, recreational opportunities, community information, and
timely seasonal updates. 
Saugatuck is a nationally recognized and award-winning community known for its natural beauty,
arts, culture, waterfront, distinctive character, and celebration of human diversity. The City's
website must effectively serve both its local community and its significant seasonal and visitor
audiences through mobile-friendly design, intuitive and task-based navigation, accessible online
services, effective search capabilities, and timely information. Through this project, the City
seeks more than a functional municipal website—it seeks an innovative, engaging, accessible,
and memorable digital experience that reflects the unique character of Saugatuck and provides
an exceptional level of service to everyone who interacts with the City. Simply stated, the City
wants a website as exceptional as Saugatuck itself. 
PROJECT BACKGROUND AND OVERVIEW 
The City of Saugatuck's current website was redesigned in 2021 using a general-purpose
website-building platform that has allowed City staff to independently create, publish, and
maintain a substantial amount of municipal information. As the City's digital presence has
grown, so have the volume and complexity of documents, meeting records, forms, public
notices, seasonal information, and online services that must be organized and maintained. 
The City seeks an experienced municipal website partner to plan, design, develop, migrate,
implement, host, secure, and provide ongoing support and maintenance for saugatuckcity.com.
The selected firm will work collaboratively with City staff to evaluate existing content and develop
an improved information architecture, modern design, and enhanced functionality. The new
website must be responsive, accessible, secure, intuitive, visually engaging, and easy for City
staff to manage. 
The website should effectively serve the City's diverse audiences, including residents and
seasonal residents; property owners; visitors; businesses; elected and appointed officials;
boards and committees; community organizations; media; contractors; permit and license
applicants; and others seeking City services and information. The website should emphasize
user-centered and task-based navigation, allowing users to quickly find services, forms, public

records, meetings, alerts, and other information without needing to understand the City's
organizational structure. 
The selected firm will be expected to improve upon—not simply replicate—the existing website.
The City welcomes professional recommendations that reduce repetitive staff maintenance,
improve search and document management, enhance accessibility and mobile usability,
support online services and future integrations, and incorporate best practices for modern
municipal websites. The City seeks a long-term digital partner capable of delivering a flexible and
scalable website that can evolve with the City's future needs. 
CURRENT WEBSITE CHALLENGES 
Over time, the City's website has grown to include a significant amount of information, resulting
in a complex navigation structure with multiple levels of menus, submenus, departments,
boards, committees, and year-specific pages. Much of the current navigation is organized
around the City's organizational structure rather than the tasks users are trying to accomplish.
This can require users to know which department, board, or commission is responsible for a
service before locating the information they need. Long, information-heavy pages and a
homepage containing numerous competing priorities can also make frequently requested
information more difficult to identify quickly. 
The growing volume of City records presents additional challenges. Years of agendas, packets,
minutes, videos, forms, plans, reports, ordinances, budgets, and other documents are
maintained across individual webpages, links, and annual archives. Forms and applications are
also available through a combination of PDFs, City-hosted forms, external forms, and third-party
resources. As this content continues to grow, improved site-wide search, centralized document
management, and a more organized approach to forms and public records are increasingly
important. 
The current structure also requires considerable manual maintenance by City staff. Meeting
records, seasonal information, schedules, election information, annual documents, and other
time-sensitive content require frequent updates. Information appearing in multiple locations
may need to be updated separately rather than entered once and automatically displayed
wherever appropriate. The redesign provides an opportunity to inventory, consolidate, archive,
and reorganize existing content while reducing repetitive administrative tasks. 
Finally, the City's digital needs have evolved beyond those of a general-purpose website
platform. The website must effectively serve year-round and seasonal residents, property
owners, businesses, visitors, applicants, voters, meeting participants, and other users with
varying needs and devices. The new website presents an opportunity to improve mobile usability,
accessibility, search functionality, content management, automation, integrations, and online
services while providing a more flexible municipal platform capable of supporting the City's
future needs.

NEW WEBSITE OBJECTIVES AND REQUIRED CAPABILITIES 
•   Intuitive, User-Centered Navigation : Create a simplified information architecture based on
what users are trying to accomplish rather than requiring users to understand the City's
organizational structure. Provide task-based navigation and clear pathways to frequently
requested information, services, forms, and documents. 
•   Responsive Design, Performance, and Mobile Accessibility:   Provide a fully responsive
website optimized for current major browsers and common desktop, tablet, and mobile
devices. Optimize photographs, graphics, video, and other media to maintain visual quality
while providing fast page loading and strong website performance. 
•   Distinctive Saugatuck Design:   Create a modern, visually engaging digital presence that
reflects Saugatuck's unique character, natural resources, waterfront, arts, culture, and
community identity. The City seeks a website that is not only functional but as exceptional as
the community it represents. 
•   Accessibility:   Conform to WCAG 2.1 Level AA and applicable ADA requirements. Conduct
accessibility testing, address identified issues, provide remediation documentation, and
provide guidance and training to help City staff maintain accessibility after launch. 
•   Content Management System (CMS) and Efficient Administration : Provide a secure,
intuitive CMS that allows authorized City staff to create, edit, schedule, publish, archive, and
manage content without HTML or specialized technical knowledge. The CMS should support
role-based permissions, workflows, audit logs, version history, rollback capabilities, and
multiple editors. Content should be structured so information can be entered once and
displayed automatically in appropriate areas of the website, reducing repetitive staff
maintenance. 
•   Centralized Meeting and Calendar Management:   Provide a unified calendar filterable by
department, board, commission, committee, event type, or other category. Meeting
functionality should support agendas, packets, minutes, notices, video links, recurring
meetings, and automated organization and archiving of meeting records. 
•   Advanced Site and Document Search:   Provide fast, accurate, intuitive site-wide search
capable of indexing webpages, PDFs, forms, meeting records, and other approved content.
Search functionality should appropriately manage archived, expired, or removed content in
accordance with City requirements. 
•   Centralized Document and Media Management:   Provide centralized libraries for
documents, photographs, graphics, video, and other media with logical organization,
metadata, accessibility support, bulk-management capabilities, and tools for identifying
broken links. 
•   Forms and Online Services:   Provide a centralized Forms & Applications Center supporting
downloadable and fillable forms, secure online forms and surveys, file uploads, confirmation
notifications, exportable data, and department-specific workflows where approved by the
City. The vendor should identify how sensitive information submitted through online forms
will be protected.

•   Online Payment Services:   Provide a secure, mobile-friendly payment portal or integration
allowing users to conveniently make online payments for applicable City services, permits,
fees, taxes, recreation, and other charges. The solution should integrate with existing or
future City payment providers, provide payment confirmations, and clearly identify
transaction fees, third-party fees, and recurring costs. 
•   News, Public Notices, Alerts, and Subscriptions:   Provide a structured system for
publishing City news, public notices, emergency or priority alerts, and other time-sensitive
information. Support scheduling and expiration of content and provide or integrate opt-in
email and SMS notifications, newsletter distribution, list management, reusable templates,
consent controls, and unsubscribe/opt-out management. All associated third-party and
recurring costs should be clearly identified. 
•   Department and Staff Information:   Provide standardized department profiles containing
services, staff contacts, telephone numbers, frequently asked questions, forms, and related
resources. Staff and contact information should be centrally managed whenever possible so
updates automatically appear throughout the website. 
•   Third-Party Integrations:   Support current and future integration or embedding of City
systems and services, including GIS and mapping, social media, ordinances, parcel and tax
records, recreation software, shared calendars, video, and other approved third-party
applications. The solution should be flexible enough to accommodate additional integrations
as City needs evolve.
